easy.heading: A Gentle Start With The Basics
easy.body:
I kicked things off by looking at the Sum 0 region. Since it covers four cells from [3,0] to [3,3], I knew every single one of those had to be a zero. It is always a relief to find those zeros early on! Then I moved to the Less than 6 constraint at [4,3]. Since the cell [3,3] right above it was already a zero from my first step, I just had to make sure the domino I placed there fit the total. It made that corner feel much more manageable.

The Sum 17 region at the top left was the real challenge for me. With three cells at [0,0], [1,0], and [2,0] to work with, I needed some heavy hitters. I ended up using parts of the [6,5] and [6,0] dominoes to get that high total. Once those big numbers were in place, the rest of the board at [0,3] and [1,3] filled itself in quite naturally. It felt like putting together a small jigsaw puzzle once the corners were done!

medium.heading: Stepping Up The Logic
medium.body:
This one felt a bit more like a balancing act compared to the easy one. I started with the Sum 1 region at [2,2]. That is a very specific clue, so I knew I had to place a 1 there right away. From there, I looked at the Equals region at [2,3], [2,4], and [3,4]. Since they all have to be the same, I had to look through my available dominoes to see which numbers I had at least three of to fill those spots.

The Sum 8 constraint at [2,0] and [3,0] was another great anchor point. I used part of the [2,0] and [6,1] dominoes there. It fits perfectly and leaves the neighboring Equals region at [0,0] and [1,0] easy to solve because those two cells just have to match. I finished up by double-checking the long Sum 8 row at the top spanning [0,1] to [0,4]. It took a second to make sure the various domino halves all added up correctly without breaking any rules.

hard.heading: Navigating The Big Grid
hard.body:
Wow, today's hard puzzle really kept me on my toes! The standout feature was that huge Unequal region in the middle involving cells like [1,1], [2,0], and [3,0]. With seven cells that all have to be different numbers, it felt like a game of Sudoku hidden inside a domino puzzle. I had to be so careful not to repeat any digits from 0 to 6 in those spots. I actually left that area for last and focused on the edges first to see what numbers were left over.

I found a lot of success starting with the Sum 0 at [1,4] and the two Sum 12 regions. For the Sum 12 at [2,4], [3,4], and [4,4], I knew I needed some of my highest dominoes like the [6,6] or [5,5]. Once those high numbers were locked in, it narrowed down what was left for the Unequal zone. The breakthrough came when I realized the Sum 9 region at the bottom left could only be a few combinations, which finally let me finish the tricky center piece.

explanation.tips: Always look for the Sum 0 or Sum 1 regions first because they have very few options and give you an easy start. It is also helpful to count how many of each number you have left in your domino pile to see what can fit in the Equals regions. If you get stuck, try looking at the very large sum targets since they usually require specific high-value dominoes like the double-six.
explanation.learned:
I learned that the Unequal regions are actually your best friend even though they look scary at first. They force you to use a variety of numbers, which helps you track which dominoes are still available in your tray. 

I also noticed that high sum regions almost always require the [6,6] or [5,5] dominoes, so I should save those for the big targets instead of using them early in smaller sums. It's all about resource management!

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You solve it by placing dominoes on the grid so that the number of dots, or pips, matches the rules for each colored region, such as sums or equal values.

faqs.question: What does an empty region mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region means there are no special math rules for those cells, but you still have to fill them with a domino that fits the rest of the board.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be rotated in the Pips game?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can place dominoes either horizontally or vertically to fill the grid and satisfy the region constraints.

faqs.question: What is an unequal region in Pips?
faqs.answer: An unequal region is a group of cells where every single cell must contain a different number of pips, with no repeats allowed.

faqs.question: Where can I find the daily Pips solution?
faqs.answer: You can find help by checking the sum targets in each region and comparing your remaining dominoes to the available empty spaces on the grid.
